Yusuf: No, that's fair, that's fair. Different strokes.
Gemma: And to be honest, with an eleven-year-old you just want an easy life. She's starting high school in September and the uniform alone has cost me a fortune.
Yusuf: Oh, the blazer and everything? My mum used to moan about that with all four of us.
Gemma: The blazer, the PE kit, the special socks with the logo on. Socks! I said to the lady, they're socks.
Yusuf: Mate, they got you. That's a racket, that.

Carys: I'd probably tell it worse than you would.
calls.C0462:
Gemma: Hiya! Can you hear me okay?
Craig: Yeah, fine. Craig. You alright?
Gemma: Gemma. I'm good thanks, last one of the round. Is that a Leigh scarf on your shelf?
Craig: It is, yeah. And you've got a Warriors magnet on your fridge, so this could go badly.
Gemma: Oh, it could. I'm from Wigan, my dad'd disown me if I was nice to you.
Craig: I'm in Leigh, so we're practically neighbours. Sorry.
Gemma: Ha. Lily's dad lives in Leigh, actually, so I'm over there every other Friday dropping her off.
Craig: Small world. What do you do?
Gemma: Primary teacher. Year 4. You?
Craig: Instrument tech at a water treatment works near Warrington. Sensors, control panels, that sort of thing. I'm on call this week, so fingers crossed.
Gemma: Oh, the engineer lady, Carys, she'd love you. She does flooding.
Craig: Yeah, she'd be one of the sensible ones I reckon.
Gemma: She was lovely. So have you got kids? I'm guessing from the pram there.
Craig: Ruby, she's four. Starts reception in September. Is there anything I should know? You're a teacher.
Gemma: Honestly, get her doing her own coat and shoes. Zips, buttons, all that. And put her name in everything, because thirty jumpers all look the same by October.
Craig: Coat and shoes. That's doable. Leanne'll be pleased I asked.
Gemma: And don't worry if she cries the first week. They're usually fine five minutes after you've gone. It's the parents who come out in bits. I was a mess with our Lily, and I'm a teacher, I should've known better.
Craig: Yeah, I reckon that'll be me.
Gemma: Do you do anything in the evenings, when you're not getting called out?
Craig: Five-a-side, Wednesdays. We were short again last week.
Gemma: I do netball Tuesdays. Goal defence. We lose every week but we have a laugh.
Craig: That's the main thing.
Gemma: The lad from Birmingham had never heard of a pie barm, by the way. And Carys called it a bap.
Craig: The Wolves lad called it a bap and all. I had to have words.
Gemma: Finally, somebody normal! I have one every Friday.
Craig: Saturday morning for me, from the bakery.
Gemma: Meat and potato?
Craig: Is there another kind?
Gemma: See, we can be friends. Just not on derby day.
Craig: Not on derby day. That's fair, that.
calls.C0463:
Carys: Hello. Can you hear me all right?
Tracey: Yeah. Tracey.
Carys: Carys. Nice to meet you.
Tracey: And you. Your kitchen's very tidy, I noticed that on the photo.
Carys: Oh. Thank you. It's not usually, I tidied the bit the camera can see.
Tracey: That's what I did and all. The post's still there though.
Carys: I saw the takeaway calendar. That's a proper kitchen, that.
Tracey: Friday nights. So what do you do?
Carys: Civil engineer. Flood risk, drainage, that sort of thing. For councils, mostly. And you?
Tracey: Kitchen assistant in a primary school canteen. Veg prep, the hatch, washing up. Is that what you wanted?
Carys: Yes, that's fine. Do you like it?
Tracey: It's alright. Term-time suits me. I'll stay there till I can afford to stop, if my knees hold out.
Carys: That's a plan, to be fair.
Tracey: My dad worked at Ford in Dagenham, and when it wound down he never really got over it. So I like knowing where I am.
Carys: My dad was at Shotton. The steelworks. Same thing, really. He was never quite the same after.
Tracey: No. They weren't, were they. That generation.
Carys: No.
Tracey: Is he still about, your dad?
Carys: He is, yes. Mum and dad are both near me. Mum helps with Rhys, my son, more than I'd like her to have to.
Tracey: My mum's seventy-eight. She's getting forgetful. Left the gas on last month. I go round Sundays with my sister but it's the other six days I lie awake about.
Carys: That must be hard.
Tracey: It is. Sorry, I don't normally say all that to people.
Carys: No, it's fine. I'd rather that than talking about the weather.
Tracey: You'd be good at the weather though, with floods.
Carys: I'm awful about the weather. I check river levels before bed.
Tracey: Do you? That's mad. I check Facebook for old photos of Dagenham.
Carys: Each to their own. What do you do when you're not working?
Tracey: Walk round Parsloes Park. Puzzle pages, word searches. And true crime, which I shouldn't, cos it gives me the creeps and then I can't sleep.
Carys: I read crime novels. Same problem, really, I'll be up till one finishing one.
Tracey: Steve says turn it off and I say no, I need to know who done it.
Carys: Yeah, no, you can't stop halfway. That's the whole point of it.
Tracey: Did you like the puzzle at the start?
Carys: I did, actually. I do the Saturday cryptic, so I'm used to it.
Tracey: I can't do them cryptic ones. I don't see how anyone gets them.
Carys: Honestly, it took me years. I still get stuck on one clue all week sometimes. I've just finished one that drove me mad.
Tracey: Well, you sound sensible. You seem it and all.
Carys: Thank you. So do you, if that's any help.
Tracey: It is a bit.
calls.C0464:
Yusuf: Hiya! Can you hear me alright? I'm Yusuf.
Craig: Yeah, fine. Craig.
Yusuf: Craig, nice one. Where are you, mate?
Craig: Leigh. Near Wigan.
Yusuf: Oh, you're the rugby lot then. Gemma was saying about all that, Wigan this, Warriors that.
Craig: Yeah, she's on the wrong side. Leigh Leopards. We had a chat about it.
Yusuf: Ha. I'm Villa. Football. What do you do?
Craig: Instrument tech, water treatment works near Warrington. I'm on call this week, so if my phone goes I'll have to go.
Yusuf: What, like proper emergencies?
Craig: Sometimes. Mostly a sensor playing up at three in the morning. You go out, fix it, come home.
Yusuf: Three in the morning, mate. I'd be useless. I'm an exec assistant, two directors at a property firm in Birmingham. Diaries, lunches, travel. Honestly the worst thing that happens to me is a restaurant losing a booking. Which I then have to explain. Creatively.
Craig: Creatively.
Yusuf: I've already been caught out twice today on that, so I'm not saying any more.
Craig: Fair enough.
Yusuf: Your flat looks cosy. Is that your little one in the photo?
Craig: Ruby, yeah. She's four. That's Tenby, that, on the beach. Last summer.
Yusuf: Lovely. And it's your place, yeah?
Craig: Renting. We want to buy, but you know. Not yet.
Yusuf: Same, we're renting in the Jewellery Quarter. Me and my girlfriend. Birmingham prices are mad.
Craig: Everywhere's mad.
Yusuf: You play any football yourself?
Craig: Five-a-side, Wednesdays, with lads from work. When they turn up.
Yusuf: No way, I'm Wednesdays as well. With my old school mates. I'm loud, I'll be honest, I'm louder than I am good. But I bring the energy.
Craig: Every team's got one.
Yusuf: Every team needs one, mate. Do you know what I mean.
Craig: I'm the one stood at the back not tracking back. Had a lad from Wolverhampton telling me off about that earlier.
Yusuf: Wolves fan? I've not had him yet. I saw his scarf on the photo, that's a problem straight away.
Craig: He was alright. Called a barm a bap, mind.
Yusuf: Mate, it is a bap. Gemma tried this on me as well, the pie barm thing.
Craig: It's a barm.
Yusuf: It's a bap. I'll say barm in Wigan, I'll say bap in Brum.
Craig: That's diplomatic.
Yusuf: That's my job, to be fair. Making everyone happy.
Craig: Suppose it is. I just fix pumps.
Yusuf: Honestly, that sounds more useful. Nobody's flooding cos I booked the wrong Lebanese place.
calls.C0465:
Gemma: Hiya! Can you hear me okay?
Tracey: Yeah. Tracey.
Gemma: Gemma. Nice to meet you, Tracey. How are you getting on with all these?
Tracey: Alright. They're quick, aren't they. You just get going and it's over.
Gemma: I know! I've been talking about pie barms all day, I think I've been rumbled as a Wiganer.
Tracey: The Birmingham lad said. He told me about it. I'd have one.
Gemma: See, that's two of us. What do you do, Tracey?
Tracey: Kitchen assistant. Primary school canteen in Dagenham.
Gemma: Oh, no way, I'm a primary teacher! Year 4. And my mum was a dinner lady before she went TA, so I've grown up hearing all about the kitchen side.
Tracey: Then you'll know the teachers are the worst at the hatch.
Gemma: Oh, we are. We're terrible. I'm sorry on behalf of all of us.
Tracey: It's fine. It's the ones who want something different every day. Jacket potato, no beans, cheese on the side. We ran out of jackets again this week and I had a teacher look at me like I'd done it on purpose.
Gemma: That's not on. Honestly, I always tell our new staff, be nice to the kitchen, they're the ones who know everything that goes on in that school.
Tracey: We do and all.
Gemma: Have you got kids yourself?
Tracey: Dean, he's twenty-seven. Moved out three years ago to Romford with his girlfriend. It was quiet after. Too quiet, if I'm honest. I didn't know what to do with myself for a bit.
Gemma: Oh, I can imagine. Lily's only eleven and she's starting high school in September, and I'm already a bit, you know. It's just me and her. I don't like thinking about her going.
Tracey: You get used to it. Sort of. He rings on a Sunday.
Gemma: That's something.
Tracey: It is. So what do you do for dinner of a night, with her?
Gemma: Tea, you mean? Sorry, I'm being northern. Spag bol, fajitas, I do a big chilli on a Sunday so I'm not cooking when I've got marking.
Tracey: Same, spag bol, shepherd's pie. Roast on a Sunday. I do a big Aldi shop and it's gone up again. Everything's gone up.
Gemma: Don't. The uniform's cost me a fortune and all. The socks have got a logo on.
Tracey: No. That's not right, that. For socks?
Gemma: I said that! I said to the lady, they're socks.
Tracey: They see you coming.
Gemma: They do. Do you watch Gogglebox? You look like a Gogglebox person, sorry, that sounds weird.
Tracey: No, I do. Every Friday with my takeaway. And the soaps. And crime documentaries, which I shouldn't.
Gemma: I fall asleep halfway through anything, I'm useless. I do love Strictly though, with my mum and Lily.
Tracey: I went to a West End show for my fiftieth. Dean paid. I still go on about it.
Gemma: Oh, that's lovely of him. That's a good lad, that.
Tracey: He is. Don't tell him I said.
Gemma: I won't.
calls.C0466:
Craig: Alright. Craig.
Carys: Hello. Carys.
Craig: Gemma said you'd be the sensible one. Flooding, is it?
Carys: That's probably fair. Flood risk and drainage, yes. What did she say about you?
Craig: Nothing, I don't think. I'm an instrument tech at a water treatment works near Warrington.
Carys: Oh, right. So we're sort of in the same trade, just at different ends of the pipe.
Craig: Yeah, that's it. You stop it going everywhere, I check it's clean when it gets to us.
Carys: What do you do day to day?
Craig: Sensors, flow meters, control panels. Calibrate them, fix them when they go. I'm on call this week, so far it's been quiet. Touch wood. Last time I was on, a level sensor at a pump station kept alarming every night at three, and it turned out to be a spider nest in the housing.
Carys: That's brilliant. I mean, it's not, at three in the morning.
Craig: It wasn't brilliant at the time, no.
Carys: Flow data's half my life, to be fair. When the models don't match the gauges, it's usually a meter somewhere that nobody's looked at for years.
Craig: That'll be one of mine, probably.
Carys: I won't hold it against you.
Craig: Where are you based?
Carys: Mold, but the office is in Chester. The A55 roadworks are a nightmare at the minute.
Craig: The M6 round Warrington's no better. Every morning.
Carys: It's always the same bit, isn't it.
Craig: Always. We were in North Wales last summer, actually. Tenby, well, that's South, but we came back through. That's the photo behind me, our Ruby on the beach.
Carys: I did wonder. She looks like she's having a good time.
Craig: She'd have stayed all day. She's four. Starts reception in September. Gemma told me to get her doing her own coat and shoes.
Carys: Good advice. I remember that stage. Rhys is sixteen now, mocks coming up. Very relaxed about it.
Craig: Unlike you?
Carys: Unlike me. You've been talking to people.
Craig: Bit of a guess, that.
Carys: It's a good guess. Do you get out walking at all, or is it all callouts?
Craig: The Lakes a couple of times a year, and Pennington Flash with Ruby. Nothing big. You?
Carys: Moel Famau most weekends. I'm out early before the cloud comes in. And I swim before work.
Craig: Before work? That's commitment.
Carys: It's habit more than anything. If I stop, I won't start again.
Craig: That's me with five-a-side. I'm thirty-five, if I miss two weeks I'll never go back.
Carys: Yeah, no, I believe that.
Craig: That's about it really. Nice to meet someone who knows what a flow meter is.
